notes.meaning: Ninety-five people returned whose family roots were tied to the town of Gibeon. Gibeon was an ancient town located north of Jerusalem. This entry marks a shift in the register, moving from lists of family ancestors to lists of the towns where the people settled.

These verses record the men returning to Bethlehem, Netophah, Anathoth, and Beth-azmaveth. Bethlehem was the ancestral home of King David, and Anathoth was the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah. By listing these towns, Nehemiah showed that families were returning to reclaim and rebuild life in their old tribal homelands.

Over thirteen hundred people returned to settle in Kiriath-jearim, Chephirah, Beeroth, Ramah, and Geba. These were historic towns belonging to the tribe of Benjamin, just north of Jerusalem. Kiriath-jearim was well known in Israel's history as the town where the Ark of the Covenant rested for many years before King David brought it to Jerusalem.

Smaller groups of returnees went back to Michmash, Bethel, Ai, and a town called the other Nebo. Bethel and Ai were famous from the stories of Abraham and Joshua, while Michmash was known as the site of a great battle led by Jonathan. The second Nebo is called "the other Nebo" to avoid confusing it with another town that shared the same name.

A large group of 1,254 people belonged to the other Elam, alongside 320 members from the family of Harim. The label "the other Elam" separated this group from the earlier family of Elam mentioned in the list. These families preserved their family records carefully so they could take up their rightful place in the community.

These entries count the returnees who settled in Jericho, the plains of Lod, Hadid, and Ono, and the large family group of Senaah. Senaah was the largest group in this part of the record, counting nearly four thousand people. Listing each group showed that God was faithfully filling the land with His people once again.

The list turns to the priests, beginning with the families of Jedaiah and Immer, who totaled over two thousand men. Only four of the twenty-four priestly divisions established under King David returned from Babylon, and these were two of them. Keeping these family records was essential because only true descendants of Aaron were allowed to serve at the altar.

These verses name the other two priestly families that returned from exile, Pashhur and Harim, each numbering over one thousand men. These four groups were later reorganized back into twenty-four shifts so temple work could run smoothly all year. God preserved these lineages so proper worship and sacrifices could begin again in Jerusalem.

Only seventy-four Levites returned through the family lines of Jeshua and Kadmiel. This was a very small number compared to the thousands of priests who came back. Levites were needed to assist the priests and care for the sacred courts, making each of these willing workers deeply valuable.

These verses record the temple singers and gatekeepers who returned from Babylon. The singers from the family of Asaph were responsible for leading musical worship, while the gatekeepers guarded the doors and storehouses. Both groups were Levites who carried out specific duties needed to keep the temple running with reverence and order.

The record lists the temple servants, also known as the Nethinim, including the families of Ziha, Hasupha, Tabbaoth, Keros, Sia, and Padon. The name Nethinim means "given ones," referring to workers dedicated to helping the Levites with daily temple chores. Even though their tasks were humble, God honored their service by preserving their names in His holy record.

The list of temple servants continues with the families of Lebanah, Hagabah, Shalmai, Hanan, Giddel, and Gahar. These families left behind their settled lives in Babylon to carry out practical, everyday work in God's house. Their inclusion reminds us that every person who helps in the Lord's work is valued and remembered.
